case_results.answer:
Yes — Meridian has a structured body of work on pricing elasticity across several frameworks. Here’s the practical briefing you can walk into the meeting with:

**When to use elasticity analysis**  
Deploy it whenever the client is considering a price change larger than a routine inflation adjustment and needs to quantify the volume impact before committing. It’s most reliable in retail and consumer categories with enough transaction-level data to model demand response directly [1].

**How the calculation works — and where it goes wrong**  
- The standard “elasticity > 1 means don’t raise price” rule applies to **revenue**, not profit. For profit decisions you need the breakeven formula that incorporates contribution margin — state the margin you used [2].  
- Always report a **confidence interval**, not just a point estimate; observational retail data is noisy and a point estimate won’t survive a competent client analytics team [2].  
- **Control for promotions, seasonality, and competitor prices**. Omitting these pushes their effects into the own-price coefficient, biasing the estimate toward apparent elasticity [1, 2].  
- **Don’t apply a portfolio-average elasticity to individual SKUs** — category- and SKU-level elasticities can differ sharply, especially between private label and branded goods [1].

**Competitive response is part of the model, not an afterthought**  
Historical elasticity estimates implicitly assume competitors don’t react. For any price move large enough to trigger a competitive response, pair the elasticity analysis with **competitive pricing response modeling** [1, 5]. Common traps there: reflexive full price-matching (usually the most margin-destructive option), misclassifying a structural competitor move as tactical, and failing to think one step ahead on how the competitor will respond to your response [5].

**Broader pricing discipline**  
- Avoid **cost-plus by default** — it leaves margin on the table in differentiated segments [3].  
- Don’t use **uniform pricing across segmented customers** — it under-prices willing segments and over-prices price-sensitive ones [3].  
- **Pilot before full rollout** — full-scale changes without a test-and-learn phase create unnecessary revenue risk, especially in B2C or highly competitive B2B [3].  
- If the conversation shifts to **value-based pricing**, remember: the value story must be quantified in the buyer’s own economic terms, you shouldn’t capture 100% of quantified value (leave the buyer a reason to switch), and value models need refreshing every 2–3 years as alternatives and evidence evolve [4].

**Bottom line for the meeting**  
If the client has transaction-level data and a meaningful price change on the table, run the elasticity model with proper controls, report intervals, use the profit breakeven formula, and layer in competitive response modeling. If they’re pricing off cost or using one price for all segments, that’s the higher-leverage fix.

**Briefing: Private Label Strategy in an Inflationary Environment**

**Core insight:** Inflation reliably drives private label penetration, but the *nature* of the trade-down customer has shifted — and most retailers' strategies haven't caught up. The winning play isn't a value-tier price play; it's using this window to build genuine brand equity that converts trial into retained loyalty once price pressure eases [1].

**What's different this cycle**
Customers trading into private label now are comparing it directly to the national brands they used to buy — not to other value-tier options. If quality perception, packaging, and distinct positioning don't hold up against that bar, the trial doesn't convert to loyalty when inflation eases [1].

**Strategic implication: treat private label as a brand, not a price tier**
Retailers capturing *durable* share gains (not just cyclical bumps) share a pattern: they invest in quality perception, packaging, and distinct category positioning during the inflationary window. This builds brand equity that survives the cycle [1].

**How this connects to Meridian's pricing & cost frameworks**
- **Value-based pricing logic applies:** The "value story" for private label must be quantified in the shopper's terms — quality, experience, trust — not just price gap. A value narrative that doesn't survive buyer (shopper) scrutiny collapses at the shelf [2].
- **Don't capture 100% of the value:** Pricing private label to capture the full price gap leaves the shopper no visible reason to stay loyal once national brands re-promote. Some value share must remain with the buyer [2].
- **Value models need updating:** The quality/price perception bar moves as national brands respond and as shopper expectations evolve. A private label positioning set at peak inflation can stale within 2–3 years [2].
- **Cost transformation can fund the brand build:** If margin compression is the trigger, zero-based budgeting (ZBB) can free spend from legacy programs (e.g., inherited loyalty/print budgets) and redirect it to private label quality, packaging, and digital storytelling — a reallocation, not just a cut [3][4].
- **Competitive response discipline:** Avoid reflexive price-matching on private label vs. national brands; don't misclassify a competitor's structural private label upgrade as a temporary promo; and model second-order effects (e.g., national brand counter-moves) before locking in pricing architecture [6].

**Bottom line for the client:** Use this inflationary window to invest in private label *brand equity* — quality, packaging, distinct positioning — funded by surgical cost transformation (ZBB on legacy SG&A). Price to share value with the shopper, not extract it all. Build a value model that survives shopper scrutiny and refresh it as the competitive set evolves. That's what turns cyclical trial into structural share.

case_results.query: Client wants help refreshing their long-range strategic plan — what's our approach?
case_results.answer:
Meridian's approach to refreshing a long-range strategic plan centers on **matching the planning method to the type of uncertainty the client faces**, then structuring the portfolio of initiatives to balance near-term performance with future resilience, and embedding execution discipline from the start.

**1. Diagnose the uncertainty first — then choose the planning lens**  
If the client operates in a structurally uncertain environment — regulatory shifts, technology disruption, geopolitical or trade-policy changes, commodity volatility — **scenario planning** is the right starting point [1]. It builds a small set of internally consistent, materially different future states and stress-tests strategic choices across all of them, avoiding the fragility of single-point forecasts that understate risk [1]. This is especially critical for capital-intensive clients making long-lived, hard-to-reverse investments (e.g., new facilities, multi-year supply chain reconfigurations) [1].

**2. Structure the initiative portfolio across three horizons**  
Regardless of the planning lens, Meridian uses the **Three-Horizons Framework** to make the current allocation of investment and leadership attention explicit — and then deliberate [2]:
- **Horizon 1**: Core business defense and extension (lower risk, near-term payback)  
- **Horizon 2**: Adjacent opportunities and new business models (2–5 years to scale, higher uncertainty)  
- **Horizon 3**: Exploratory bets on a 5+ year horizon (high uncertainty, option value)  

Most organizations default to 90%+ in Horizon 1 [2]. The refresh should assess whether that balance is intentional or a drift — and set a **target allocation** calibrated to the client’s industry clock-speed and competitive threat profile [2]. A stable industry may justify Horizon-1-heavy; a disrupted one needs material Horizons 2/3 investment, even at near-term margin cost [2].

**3. Govern each horizon differently**  
Horizon 1 initiatives warrant standard ROI and payback discipline [2]. Horizon 3 bets require different metrics — **learning velocity, option value** — because conventional ROI hurdles kill legitimate long-horizon options before they can prove out [2].

**4. Sequence the roadmap to sustain sponsorship and adaptability**  
Drawing from digital transformation roadmap principles, the plan must avoid two traps [3]:
- **Leading with visible, customer-facing work** before foundational dependencies are ready — creating expensive-to-scale wins  
- **All foundation, no visible value** — losing sponsorship over a multi-year horizon  

The roadmap should include **built-in reassessment points** so it doesn’t become a fixed plan followed past its relevance [3].

**5. Embed change management from day one**  
A refreshed strategy fails if communication is poorly sequenced [4]. Meridian’s approach:
- **Sequence by audience readiness**, not convenience — high-influence and directly affected stakeholders hear first, directly [4]  
- **Tailor message and channel**: leadership gets strategic rationale and cascading role; frontline gets practical, personal impact via trusted managers [4]  
- **Build two-way channels** to surface concerns early and test resistance assumptions [4]  
- **Plan the silence** — deliberate cadence of updates (even “no new decision”) prevents rumor-filled vacuums [4]

**6. If cost transformation is part of the refresh, treat it as a structural reset — not a cut**  
Cost work must have a **delivery plan with named owners and tracked milestones** — analysis alone doesn’t realize savings [5]. Avoid **cutting below the capability floor** needed to serve customers, which triggers bounce-back with service-quality damage [5]. Always **benchmark against peers** so targets are defensible, not arbitrary [5].

**7. If market entry or expansion is in scope, follow the four-stage gate**  
- **Opportunity framing**: agree on success criteria (revenue, share, strategic rationale) upfront to prevent scope creep [6]  
- **Market sizing**: triangulate TAM/SAM/SOM with top-down and bottom-up methods [6]  
- **Competitive landscape mapping**: identify incumbents, strength, white space — reveals if “opportunity” is contested [6]  
- **Entry mode recommendation**: organic, partnership/JV, acquisition — or no-go — based on sizing, competition, risk appetite, and capability gaps [6]

**In practice**: A long-range plan refresh typically opens with **scenario planning (if uncertainty is structural)** or **three-horizons portfolio review (if the challenge is growth stall or disruption risk)** — often both. The output isn’t just a document; it’s a **governed portfolio with horizon-appropriate metrics, a sequenced roadmap with reassessment gates, a stakeholder communication cadence, and — where relevant — a cost reset or market entry plan with delivery rigor baked in**.

case_results.query: Getting staffed on a market entry study — get me up to speed on our approach.
case_results.answer:
Meridian's market entry approach is a structured, four-stage framework that moves from decision framing through to a conditional go/no-go recommendation. The methodology is designed to avoid the most common failure mode: jumping straight to market sizing without first agreeing on what "success" looks like for the specific client [1].

**Stage 1: Frame the decision & agree the success bar**  
Before any modeling, the team must secure a written, quantitative success threshold from the client (e.g., a revenue or share target). Gate 1 of the Go/No-Go Quick Reference Card makes this explicit: the engagement fails this gate if the client says "we'll know it when we see it" [4]. This success bar then anchors every subsequent analysis — without it, a TAM number has no decision attached to it [1].

**Stage 2: Size the opportunity with triangulated, defensible estimates**  
Market sizing follows a TAM → SAM → SOM funnel [5]:
- **TAM**: total category demand, unconstrained by the client's capabilities.
- **SAM**: the portion the client could realistically serve given geography, regulation, and product fit.
- **SOM**: the portion the client can realistically capture given competition, go-to-market capability, and time horizon.

You must build **two independent estimates** — top-down (from published data, filtered by addressable logic) and bottom-up (from unit economics: potential customers × penetration × ARPU). If they diverge by more than ~30%, the gap itself is a finding; do not simply average them [5]. Present a **range with sensitivity cases** (conservative/base/aggressive) and call out the assumption driving the most variance [5]. Gate 2 requires top-down and bottom-up to be within ~30% [4].

**Stage 3: Map the competitive landscape to find defensible white space**  
This stage assesses likely incumbent response — price cuts, marketing spend increases, product roadmap acceleration — because a market that looks open can close quickly if incumbents are well-capitalized and motivated to defend share [2]. The output is a judgment on whether a defensible position exists. Gate 3 passes only when "an identified, defensible position exists"; it fails when "every segment is contested by a stronger incumbent" [4].

**Stage 4: Select the entry mode based on the binding constraint**  
Entry mode (JV, acquisition, greenfield) is chosen last, once you have a sized opportunity and a competitive read [3]. The competitive landscape mapping identifies the binding constraint (e.g., distribution access, regulatory relationships, speed to market) that shapes the mode choice [3]. If acquisition is recommended, the workstream connects to M&A integration (Day 1 readiness) and commercial due diligence for pre-acquisition validation [3].

**The Go/No-Go decision is rarely binary**  
Most engagements land on a **conditional recommendation** — enter via partnership, enter a sub-segment first, wait 18 months — rather than a clean yes/no [1]. The final gate (Gate 4) tests whether capability gaps (distribution, regulatory, brand) are closable in the time available; it fails if the gap requires a capability the client has never built [4].

**Key pitfalls to avoid**  
- Sizing before framing the success bar [1]  
- Ignoring capability gaps — a large, attractive market can still be a bad entry if the client lacks the required assets [1]  
- Forcing a binary go/no-go too early; conditional paths are the norm [1]  
- Relying on a single sizing method or presenting a point estimate without sensitivity [5]  
- Burying competitive response risk; incumbents can close an open market quickly [2]

case_results.query: Client is asking whether their AI investments are actually delivering value — what do we have to frame that?
case_results.answer:
Most enterprises are measuring AI value the wrong way — and the sources show exactly how to reframe the question.

**The core problem: ROI theater, not value measurement**  
Nearly every AI initiative arrives with a demand for a quantified ROI case, but most are built on a measurement frame borrowed from traditional automation that doesn't fit how AI-driven productivity gains actually appear [1]. The result is systematically misleading answers — not because financial discipline is wrong, but because the metric is mismatched to the mechanism.

**What credible evaluation looks like**  
Organizations getting this right have moved away from a single blended enterprise-wide ROI number — which averages high- and low-value deployments and obscures where value is concentrated — toward a **workflow-by-workflow view** that traces specific, well-scoped deployments to specific, measurable downstream business outcomes [1]. They use **capacity-reallocation and quality-adjusted metrics**, not throughput alone. This is more analytically demanding and produces a less clean board-level headline, but it reveals which use cases genuinely drive value (informing where to double down) and which consume investment without commensurate return — a distinction a single ROI figure systematically obscures [1].

**The maturity signal: subtraction, not addition**  
The clearest signal of real AI maturity (Stage 5 in Meridian's model) is **subtractive**: the organization has retired deployments that didn't deliver [2]. An organization that has never retired a GenAI deployment either has an implausible hit rate or isn't measuring honestly. Most enterprises self-report "scaling" but operate at "structured experimentation" — adoption (seat licenses, query volumes, pilot counts) is easy to count; maturity (governance, measurement, workflow integration) is not [2].

**What this means for the client conversation**  
Don't ask "What's our AI ROI?" Ask instead:
- Which specific workflows have deployed AI, and what downstream business outcome does each trace to?
- What capacity was reallocated or quality improved — not just throughput gained?
- Which deployments have been retired, and why?
- Is value tracking at the portfolio level, with a standard governance process (not a special AI process) for new use cases [2]?

The banks making fastest progress in risk functions didn't start with flashy pilots — they started with a narrow, well-scoped use case, built groundedness and governance in from day one, and used that first deployment to build organizational trust before expanding [5]. The same discipline applies here: **prove measurement works before scaling the portfolio.**
